extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proof writing and elementary set theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance, definitions, and proof techniques for elementary set theory (subsets, power set, union/intersection, complements, set-difference, Cartesian products, indexed families) together with recommended proof-writing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a subset by element method
rubrics_metrics.description: To show A ⊆ B, assume a ∈ A and then work towards showing that a ∈ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume the hypothesis is true and show the conclusion (footnote 83 notes that if a ∉ A the implication (a ∈ A) ⇒ (a ∈ C) is vacuously true). The authors demonstrate this by letting a ∈ A, using known subset relations (e.g. A ⊆ B) to deduce a ∈ B. Scratchwork can be more involved, but the final written proof should be succinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove set equality by mutual inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove A = B show both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard biconditional proof strategy: prove each implication in turn. Do scratchwork to explore directions, then write a concise two-part proof showing each inclusion (examples throughout the text follow this pattern).

rubrics_metrics.name: Power set definition
rubrics_metrics.description: The power set 𝒫(A) is the set of all subsets of A; X ∈ 𝒫(A) ⇐⇒ X ⊆ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note that elements of 𝒫(A) are themselves sets (hence use capital X for elements of 𝒫). Use this definition when manipulating or proving statements about power sets (e.g. counting or inclusion arguments).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving inclusions of power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: To show 𝒫(A) ⊆ 𝒫(B) from A ⊆ B: assume X ∈ 𝒫(A) so X ⊆ A, then use A ⊆ B to deduce X ⊆ B, hence X ∈ 𝒫(B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prior results about subsets (e.g. Result 8.1.4) to carry subset relations through; treat X as a set (capital letter) and reduce power-set inclusion to ordinary subset inclusion in the scratchwork before writing the succinct proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving converse for power sets
rubrics_metrics.description: To deduce A ⊆ B from 𝒫(A) ⊆ 𝒫(B): note A ∈ 𝒫(A), so A ∈ 𝒫(B), hence A ⊆ B by definition of power set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This uses the fact that a set is an element of its own power set; explicit recognition of which objects are sets vs elements is important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notational conventions for sets vs elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Use uppercase letters for sets (A, B, X) and lowercase for elements (a, x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: when proving things about elements of the power set use X rather than x since X is itself a set (footnote 85: 'The power of good notational conventions!'). Consistent naming avoids confusion when elements may or may not belong to particular sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions of union and intersection (and logical parallels)
rubrics_metrics.description: A ∪ B = {x | x ∈ A or x ∈ B} (inclusive 'or'); A ∩ B = {x | x ∈ A and x ∈ B}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can rewrite these as (x ∈ A ∪ B) ⇐⇒ (x ∈ A) ∨ (x ∈ B) and (x ∈ A ∩ B) ⇐⇒ (x ∈ A) ∧ (x ∈ B). Be careful: 'or' and 'and' are used in their precise logical senses in mathematical definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning: do not confuse set and logical operators
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressions mixing set and logical notation are invalid: when A and B are sets, 'A ∨ B' and 'A ∧ B' do not make sense; similarly, if P and Q are statements, 'P ∪ Q' and 'P ∩ Q' do not make sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep operators in the appropriate domain: sets use ∪, ∩, complements; statements use ∨, ∧, negation. The warning (8.2.3) emphasizes correct notation and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venn diagrams as heuristic, not proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Venn diagrams help visualise set relationships but are not proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams as scratchwork to understand and explore problems; a valid proof must show the result for every choice of sets, not just the drawn example (remark and multiple examples stress this point).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use LHS/RHS shorthand for lengthy manipulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Refer to the left-hand side and right-hand side of an equality as 'LHS' and 'RHS' to avoid repeating long expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This shorthand reduces clutter in calculations and indicates when one side stays fixed while you transform the other. It is common mathematician style (Remark 8.2.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic membership lemmas for union/intersection
rubrics_metrics.description: Helpful small results: if x ∈ A then x ∈ A ∪ B; if x ∈ A ∩ B then x ∈ A; if x ∉ A ∪ B then x ∉ A and x ∉ B; if x ∉ A ∩ B then x ∉ A or x ∉ B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State contrapositives explicitly; these simple implications are used frequently to streamline proofs (Lemma 8.4.5 and its contrapositive list).

rubrics_metrics.name: DeMorgan's laws for sets
rubrics_metrics.description: For A, B ⊂ U: ¯(A ∩ B) = ¯A ∪ ¯B and ¯(A ∪ B) = ¯A ∩ ¯B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are standard transformations for complements used to simplify or re-express set formulas; proofs typically use membership characterisations and lemmas above (Theorem 8.4.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distributive laws for sets
rubrics_metrics.description: A ∪ (B ∩ C) = (A ∪ B) ∩ (A ∪ C) and A ∩ (B ∪ C) = (A ∩ B) ∪ (A ∩ C). Similar distributivity holds for Cartesian products: A × (B ∩ C) = (A × B) ∩ (A × C) etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These laws look like distributivity in arithmetic and are used to rearrange expressions; proofs are membership-based (Theorem 8.4.3 and examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-difference identities
rubrics_metrics.description: A − B = A ∩ ¯B, and related equalities such as A − (B ∩ C) = (A − B) ∪ (A − C), A − (B ∪ C) = (A − B) ∩ (A − C), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive these using definitions and DeMorgan/distributive laws; they are practical rewriting tools (Theorem 8.4.4 and Example 8.4.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cartesian product definition and ordered-pair properties
rubrics_metrics.description: A × B = {(a, b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B}. Ordered pairs have (a, b) ≠ (b, a) unless a = b, and (a, b) = (c, d) only when a = c and b = d.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remember order matters in Cartesian products; when proving product equalities treat elements as ordered pairs and reason component-wise (Definition 8.3.2, Example 8.3.3).

rubrics_metrics.name: Technique for proving equalities involving Cartesian products
rubrics_metrics.description: When proving e.g. A × (B ∪ C) = (A × B) ∪ (A × C) take a generic element (x,y) ∈ A × (B ∪ C) and show it lies in RHS by considering whether y ∈ B or y ∈ C, and conversely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make ordered-pair structure explicit in scratchwork and later in the final succinct proof; the text uses this pattern in Example 8.4.8.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indexed unions and intersections (quantifier forms)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an indexed family {A_k}: ⋂_{k=m}^M A_k = {x | ∀ j ∈ {m,…,M}, x ∈ A_j} and ⋃_{k=m}^M A_k = {x | ∃ j ∈ {m,…,M} with x ∈ A_j}; similarly for infinite/index sets and for arbitrary indexing set S use ∀s∈S and ∃s∈S quantifiers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate index notation to quantifiers when reasoning about membership; explicit quantifier understanding clarifies infinite intersections/unions (Definitions 8.5.1 and 8.5.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility and caution in choosing index sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Index sets need not be natural numbers — they can be rationals, reals or any set; write ∩_{s∈S} A_s for general indexing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When indexing by uncountable sets (e.g. reals) you cannot write out the list; be careful with notation and with any intuition based on sequences (Remark 8.5.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful use of limit/intuitive reasoning with indexed sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not infer intersection/union results from limit intuition alone — use definitions. Example: intersection of (-1/n,1/n) for n≥1 contains 0 (not empty) even though intervals shrink to 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work from the precise definitions (∀ or ∃ over indices) rather than informal limit reasoning when deciding membership in infinite intersections/unions (Example 8.5.3 and 8.5.6 commentary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference previous results explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: When using earlier lemmas or theorems, refer to them by number or as 'previous result' if nearby.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit citations improve clarity and avoid re-proving facts; the text suggests numbering results or saying 'previous result' when the result is nearby (footnote 86).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable naming to avoid misleading membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose neutral variable names where appropriate (e.g. use x rather than b or c when the element might belong to multiple sets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using neutral letters reduces the implication that an element belongs to a particular named set; the text exemplifies this in proofs where x is used instead of b or c (Example 8.2.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof-writing workflow: scratchwork then concise write-up
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform detailed scratchwork (exploring cases, computations) and then write a succinct, polished proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors model doing scratchwork with twists and turns, then producing the succinct 'Proof.' box for final presentation. This is advocated repeatedly: 'Oof! ... write it up nicely.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use case analysis and Euclidean division where appropriate
rubrics_metrics.description: Use case splits (e.g. ℓ = 3j, 3j+1, 3j+2) or Euclidean division to reason about divisibility or modular possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case analysis is a standard tool when direct algebraic deduction is awkward; the example proving B ∩ C ⊆ A uses three cases for ℓ to show divisibility by 3 (Example 8.2.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contrapositives to simplify membership arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Many useful implications are easier to apply in contrapositive form (e.g. x ∉ A ⇒ x ∉ A ∩ B).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State contrapositives explicitly when they are helpful (Lemma 8.4.5 lists both forward statements and their contrapositives).
